h1:
10 New Places to Visit in Chiang Mai
Off the Beaten Path
intro: Chiang Mai gets new places to visit popping up almost every season — cafes deep in the forest, wide grassland plateaus, viewpoints hardly anyone reaches yet, and western-style farms close to town. We've picked 10 spots that are still open for real in 2026. Some only just got popular, some have been around a while but still see few visitors. We'll tell you straight which ones are easy to reach and which take some work, who each one suits, plus locations, opening hours, and rough entry fees — so you can plan a trip that doesn't just follow the crowd.

blocks.html: The spots on this list spread across three rings. The inner ring, within about an hour of town, is the cowboy ranch and the forest cafe you can drive out to in the morning and be back by evening with no trouble. Further out, toward Mae Rim and Mae Taeng, are the plateau spots and the fantasy-themed gardens that work well for an overnight stay. The outer ring — Doi Tao, Mae Chaem, and Chom Thong — are full-day nature trips that take a bit of preparation. We've ordered them from nearest to farthest and from easy to rugged, so you can pick based on the energy and time you've got.

blocks.text: Pick a new spot by your style

items.name: You want a chilled cafe
items.blurb: The Giant treehouse cafe, or Dan Tevada's fantasy forest garden — great for photos, no hiking needed

items.name: You want wide views for photos
items.blurb: Mon Jam in Mae Rim, or the Mon Cham skywalk — sea of mist and flower gardens in the cool season

items.name: You want real nature and adventure
items.blurb: Pha Khun Tae, Mae Sap Cave, Tat Jo Waterfall — rough roads but quiet, with few people

items.name: You want an easy family day out
items.blurb: Cowboy Army, a sheep farm near town — kids can feed the animals and ride horses

blocks.text: 10 new places that are still open in 2026

blocks.html: Before you set off, two things worth knowing for everyone. First, a lot of the plateau spots and secret viewpoints sit on mountain roads that are hard for a sedan to climb — check your car and the route first, and for some you'll need to switch to a motorbike or a local vehicle for the final stretch. Second, several shops and gardens close on Mondays or only open seasonally, so it's safer to call ahead before you go, especially if you're driving a long way.

items.name: The Giant Chiangmai — cafe in a giant tree (Mae On)
items.blurb: A cafe built up in a huge tree in the forest of Ban Pok. Sip your coffee and you feel like you're floating above the treetops, looking out over green ridges and morning mist. It was renovated with a new zone opening in early 2026, with rope-descent and forest-walk activities to choose from. It's been popular for a long time, but plenty of people still haven't made it out here. Go in the morning for the best view, before it gets crowded.
items.meta: Ban Pok, Mae On District · open Tue–Sun, roughly 08:30–17:00 (closed Mondays)

items.name: Dan Tevada — fantasy forest garden (Mae Taeng)
items.blurb: A forest garden styled in a tropical-meets-Japanese mood, with man-made waterfalls, rock caves, wooden bridges, and a green stream running through big old trees. Walking it feels like wandering into a storybook forest. There's a cafe, a restaurant, and goat and rabbit pens where kids can feed the animals — shady and cool, good for all ages. It sits right next to the Mae Taeng post office, under an hour's drive from town.
items.meta: San Maha Phon, Mae Taeng District · open daily 08:00–18:00

items.name: Mon Jam — a slice of Europe on the plateau (Mae Rim)
items.blurb: A spot up on the Pong Yaeng plateau dressed up to feel like a European town, with a wide lake, a sailboat you can hop on for photos, European-style buildings, vintage cars, and flower gardens in full bloom during the cool season. The key thing: Mon Jam opens seasonally, mostly during the late-year-to-early-year high season, so always check its page before you go. Dress up and you can shoot to your heart's content.
items.meta: Pong Yaeng, Mae Rim District · open seasonally (high season)

items.name: Cowboy Army Riding Club — cowboy ranch near town (Mae Rim)
items.blurb: A farm and restaurant on the grounds of an army veterinary unit in Don Kaeo — a pretty Doi Suthep viewpoint that's very close to town. There's a sheep farm where you can feed and wash the sheep, horseback riding into the forest, ATVs, and bikes. The restaurant serves steak, barbecue, pizza, burgers, and coffee. Good for spending the whole day with kids.
items.meta: Don Kaeo, Mae Rim District · farm 08:00–18:00, restaurant 10:00–21:00
items.price: Activities start in the low hundreds · meals ฿120–350 each

items.name: Mon Cham skywalk — bamboo bridge through flower gardens
items.blurb: A long bamboo walkway along the Mon Cham ridge that runs through flower beds and terraced fields, open for strolling above layered mountain ridges. In the cool season there's morning mist and cool-climate flowers blooming all over the beds. It's in the Mon Cham area, which has cafes and Hmong-costume photo spots to carry on to. About an hour's drive from town.
items.meta: Mon Cham, Pong Yaeng, Mae Rim District · open daily, daytime

items.name: Kiew Fin viewpoint, Mae Kampong — panorama above the village
items.blurb: A viewpoint on the ridge above Mae Kampong village, looking out over layered green mountains as far as you can see. The air is cool year-round, with morning mist in the cool season. It's a short walk up from the parking area. Pair it with a tour of Mae Kampong village, the waterfall, and the cafes in the village all in one day. It's a corner people are starting to discover but isn't as packed as Mon Cham yet.
items.meta: Ban Mae Kampong, Mae On District · accessible anytime, best view in the morning

items.name: Kowit Krathom Plai Na — farmstay among terraced fields (Mae Chaem)
items.blurb: A wooden-cabin farmstay in the Mae Chaem valley, wrapped in terraced rice fields with a private stream you can soak in. The atmosphere is quiet and peaceful, with mist drifting in the morning. The standout photo spot is the field that juts out into a sharp pointed tier. The view changes with the season: transplanting in July, green rice in August–September, golden rice in October–November. Staying overnight has more atmosphere than a morning-to-evening visit.
items.meta: Tha Pha, Mae Chaem District · farmstay, book ahead

items.name: Doi Tao Lake savanna grassland — wide plain behind the dam
items.blurb: A plain behind the Bhumibol Dam where the water has dropped enough to turn into a wide green grassland of several thousand rai, looking like a savanna. Locals use it to graze livestock, and at night you can pitch a tent and count the stars. The area is wide and very open, good for campers after an unusual atmosphere. Best to go in the late-rainy-to-early-cool season while the grass is still green, and bring plenty of water and supplies.
items.meta: Tha Duea, Doi Tao District · accessible anytime, best in the late rainy–cool season
items.price: No entry fee · pitch your own tent

items.name: Pha Khun Tae, Doi Pha Khao Noi — secret viewpoint for the rugged (Chom Thong)
items.blurb: A peak in the Ban Khun Tae area with a panorama of green forest. The standout is a cliff that looks like a cave mouth, where you can walk along and sit for photos, with a sky full of stars at night. The route is fairly rough — narrow, steep, and slippery — and cars can't make it, so you'll have to walk or hire a motorbike for the final stretch. Suited to the adventurous who don't mind the effort. Still very few people.
items.meta: Ban Khun Tae, Chom Thong District · start from Ban Khun Tae School
items.price: No entry fee · camping on the plateau is allowed

items.name: Mae Sap Cave + Tat Jo Waterfall — two nature spots still off most radars
items.blurb: Mae Sap Cave in Samoeng is known as the rainbow cave, because the rock walls have bands of yellow, orange, red, and brown alternating like a rainbow curtain. It's under the care of Khun Khan National Park, so bring a flashlight. Tat Jo Waterfall in Chom Thong, meanwhile, is a waterfall deep in the forest where the water threads through a gap in the rock like a cave hollow, throwing off green-gold glints when the sun hits it. Both still see few visitors and suit those who like getting into the forest.
items.meta: Mae Sap Cave, Samoeng Tai, Samoeng District 08:00–17:00 · Tat Jo Waterfall, Ban Pae, Chom Thong District
items.price: No entry fee (small park fee at some spots)

blocks.title: What to know about the roads before heading up the plateaus
blocks.html: Spots like Pha Khun Tae, Mon Jam, and the Doi Tao grassland are on mountain roads where, in some stretches, a sedan struggles or can't make it at all. If you don't know the roads, rent a four-wheel drive or hire a local vehicle for the final stretch. Fill up the tank back in town because gas stations up on the plateau are hard to find, and check the forecast — rain makes the roads slippery and very dangerous.

blocks.text: Plan a trip to the new spots without wearing yourself out

blocks.html: The trick is, don't pack two far-flung spots into one day, because each one is in a different direction and means a long drive. The most enjoyable way is to split it into a near-town day and a plateau day. Take the near-town day easy; on the plateau day, head out early and get back before dark, because the mountain roads have no lights. Below is one example of an easy day that doesn't involve any hiking.

blocks.title: When it looks its best
blocks.html: The plateau spots, flower gardens, and sea of mist look their best from the late rainy season into the cool season, roughly November through February — cool air, clear skies — and the terraced fields at Mae Chaem turn golden around October through November. If you come in the rainy season the views are lush and green, but the roads are slippery and some spots may close, so check first.

blocks.text: Want a fuller trip? Tie these in with other Chiang Mai spots

blocks.html: This list focuses on new spots and corners that still see few people. If you want to round out the whole trip, just pair them with Chiang Mai's main attractions. Nature lovers can carry on to the bigger plateaus and waterfalls, cafe fans to the cafe districts in town, and culture lovers can walk the old-town temples and the craft villages. We've put together separate guides for each — see the links at the end of the article.

faq.q: Which new place in Chiang Mai is the closest to town?
faq.a: Cowboy Army Riding Club in Don Kaeo, Mae Rim District, is very close to town — just a few tens of minutes' drive from the city. It's a sheep farm and restaurant with a Doi Suthep viewpoint, where you can take kids to feed the animals and ride horses. Dan Tevada in Mae Taeng is also under an hour's drive, good for a morning-to-evening visit.

faq.q: Is Mon Jam open all year round?
faq.a: No. Mon Jam opens seasonally, mostly during the late-year-to-early-year high season when the air is cool and the flowers are blooming — it isn't open every day all year. Always check Mon Jam's page before you go to see whether it's open this round, so you don't make the trip for nothing, since it's a long drive up the Pong Yaeng plateau.

faq.q: Which spots on the list suit people who don't want to hike?
faq.a: If you'd rather not deal with rough roads, go for The Giant treehouse cafe, the Dan Tevada forest garden, the Cowboy Army ranch, and the Mon Cham skywalk. Cars reach all four and they're easy to walk around. Pha Khun Tae, the Doi Tao grassland, and Tat Jo Waterfall have rougher routes and suit the adventurous who come prepared.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Chiang Mai's new spots?
faq.a: From the late rainy season into the cool season, roughly November through February, is the prettiest — cool air, clear skies, morning mist, and cool-climate flower gardens in bloom. The terraced fields at Kowit Krathom Plai Na in Mae Chaem turn golden around October through November. In the rainy season the views are lush and green, but the roads are slippery and some spots close.

faq.q: Can you drive a sedan to Pha Khun Tae and the Doi Tao grassland?
faq.a: It's fairly tough. Pha Khun Tae in Chom Thong has a narrow, steep, and slippery route that cars can't make — you'll have to walk or hire a motorbike for the final stretch. The Doi Tao grassland is a wide plain, but parts of the access road are dirt, so a higher-clearance vehicle or a four-wheel drive is recommended, and it's best to go in the dry season rather than the rainy one.

faq.q: What do you need to bring for Mae Sap Cave?
faq.a: There's no light inside the cave, so bring your own flashlight or headlamp, wear shoes that grip on slippery ground, and allow extra time, since it's under the care of Khun Khan National Park and open roughly 08:00–17:00. The highlight is the cave wall with its rainbow-like bands of color. Go with someone who knows the way, or ask the staff before heading in.
